newsitem.title: USA: Civil rights activists arrested at DEA office.
newsitem.headline: Civil rights activists arrested at DEA office.

text.p: Four civil rights activists were arrested outside a federal building on Monday, demanding more information on reported links between the CIA and drug dealers who flooded black ghettos with cocaine in the 1980s.

The protest was the latest in a furore set off by an investigative series last month by the San Jose Mercury News, which reported that a drug pipeline between Colombia and California functioned for almost a decade with at least tacit CIA approval, funnelling profits to the CIA-backed Contras in Nicaragua.

Rev. Joseph Lowery, president of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, entertainer Dick Gregory and activists Joe Madison and Mark Thompson, were arrested by the Federal Protective Service outside the headquarters of the Drug Enforcement Agency, according to Madison's publicist, Cynthia Leslie.
The Federal Protective Service, which handles security at federal buildings, had no immediate comment.

The Justice Department, the CIA and a House of Representatives committee are investigating the series in the San Jose Mercury News. The news stories said the Contra-linked drug pipeline was the first major source of crack cocaine in Los Angeles. From there, the drug spread to the rest of the nation.
CIA Director John Deutch ordered the internal CIA probe Sept. 4 but said he believed there was "no substance" to the "allegations."

Leslie said the four activists were arrested and charged with "impeding public traffic" after forming a human chain and demanding that DEA release information about the reports. One of the major drug traffikers cited in the San Jose series has recently been a DEA drug informant.
The four would be arraigned Tuesday, she said.
Madison and Gregory were arrested after a similar protest at the CIA headquarters Sept. 11, but federal authorities later dropped the charges, Leslie said.

Earlier former DEA agent Celerino Castillo III told reporters he documented evidence of shipments of cocaine flown from Central America to the United States in the late 1980s and sent it to DEA headquarters, but no action was taken.
The San Jose Mercury News series and supporting documents have been published on the Internet's World Wide Web at the address, http://www.sjmercury.com/drugs/.
